children: Shares of three companies with mining and energy projects in Greenland surged in extended trading Friday after President Donald Trump announced a security agreement with Denmark and the Arctic territory.
Greenland Energy
jumped 119% after hours, while Greenland Mines (GLMN) rose 58% and Critical Metals
gained 20%.

The rallies appeared to reflect investor expectations that an expanded U.S. presence could bring greater political support, infrastructure investment and financing opportunities to Greenland’s resource sector. However, the agreement didn't include any announced funding, permits or commercial agreements for the three companies.

Trump said the deal would give the United States a permanent role in Greenland’s security and prevent adversaries from establishing military bases or making sensitive investments without U.S. approval. He also said the United States would begin developing a larger military presence on the island.
The agreement is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Its full terms have not been released.

Denmark and Greenland described the arrangement more narrowly than Trump. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, while Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it recognizes the territory’s interests.

For investors, the market reaction highlights how closely Greenland-focused stocks have become tied to U.S. national-security policy. The island holds deposits of rare earths, precious metals and other resources used in defense systems, electronics and energy technologies. Still, Friday’s gains were based mainly on the perceived implications of the agreement rather than any immediate improvement in the companies’ finances or projects.
Greenland Mines

Greenland Mines (GLMN) owns the Skaergaard project in southeastern Greenland, which contains gold, palladium and platinum resources. The company also recently completed its acquisition of the Sarfartoq rare-earth project in southwestern Greenland.

Sarfartoq is expected to target neodymium and praseodymium, two elements used to make permanent magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and military equipment. Greenland Mines has estimated that a higher-production scenario for the project could generate a pretax net present value of as much as $2.05 billion.
The company issued a statement Friday welcoming the security agreement and saying it reinforces Greenland’s strategic importance to the United States.
Critical Metals
Critical Metals
owns the Tanbreez rare-earth project in southern Greenland. The company describes Tanbreez as one of the world’s largest known deposits of heavy rare earth elements.

In May, Critical Metals signed a 15-year agreement to supply REalloys with rare-earth concentrate representing 15% of Tanbreez’s planned annual production. The project also has attracted interest from the U.S. Export-Import Bank as Washington seeks supply chains that are less dependent on China.

Investors may see the new security framework as reducing geopolitical uncertainty surrounding Tanbreez and improving its prospects for U.S. government assistance. The agreement itself, however, did not announce new financing for the project.
Greenland Energy
Greenland Energy
is an early-stage oil and gas explorer focused on the Jameson Land Basin in eastern Greenland. The company plans to finance exploration wells in exchange for a majority interest in the project.

Its shares registered the biggest move Friday, more than doubling in extended trading. The scale of the rally suggests speculative interest in companies offering direct exposure to Greenland rather than a response to a company-specific development.

Greenland stopped issuing new oil and gas exploration licenses in 2021 because of environmental concerns, although some older licenses remained in effect. Greenland Energy still needs regulatory approvals before conducting its planned drilling program.

That makes the company the most speculative of the three Greenland trades. A larger U.S. military and infrastructure presence could eventually improve access to remote areas, but it does not override Greenland’s permitting process or guarantee that commercial quantities of oil will be found.

Extended-hours trading can be volatile because fewer shares are available to buy and sell. The gains therefore may narrow or reverse when regular trading resumes. Investors also will be watching for the agreement’s final language and any subsequent U.S. financing, permitting or infrastructure announcements affecting Greenland’s resource projects.
